title: Saying it twice
goal: Learn what doubling a word does in Indonesian: it can make a plural, a variety (“all kinds of”), a relaxed or aimless action, or an adverb of manner — and learn when *not* to double.
bekal: shop in a traditional market with *buah-buahan, sayur-mayur, rempah-rempah*
soften and relax what you do: *lihat-lihat, jalan-jalan, cari-cari*
avoid the classic over-doubling mistake: *tiga buku*, never *tiga buku-buku*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Sabtu pagi di Beringharjo
dialogs.intro: Saturday morning. Bu Endang takes Sarah to Pasar Beringharjo, the big old market at the end of Jalan Malioboro, and steers her through the crowd with one hand on her elbow.

lines.text: Mbak, jalannya pelan-pelan saja. Beringharjo kalau Sabtu ramai sekali.
lines.id: Take it slowly, Mbak. Beringharjo is packed on Saturdays.
lines.literal: Miss, walk-the slow-slow just. Beringharjo if Saturday crowded very.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Wah, orangnya banyak banget, Bu. Semua jualan apa?
lines.id: Wow, there are so many people. What is everyone selling?
lines.literal: wow, person-the many very, Mrs. all sell what?

lines.speaker: Endang:
lines.text: Macam-macam. Di sini sayur-mayur, di belakang buah-buahan, di atas rempah-rempah.
lines.id: All sorts. Vegetables here, fruit at the back, spices upstairs.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Saya mau lihat-lihat dulu, boleh?

lines.speaker: Endang:
lines.text: Boleh, tapi jangan jauh-jauh. Nanti Mbak hilang.
lines.id: Yes, but don't wander off. You'll get lost.
lines.literal: may, but don't far-far. later Miss lost.

lines.text: Monggo, Mbak, Bu. Salaknya manis-manis, baru datang dari Sleman.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Berapa sekilo, Bu?

lines.speaker: Penjual:
lines.text: Lima belas ribu, Mbak. Boleh dicoba dulu.
lines.id: Fifteen thousand. Try one first.
lines.literal: five teen thousand, Miss. may is-tried first.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Hmm, manis sekali! Saya ambil dua kilo, ya.
lines.id: Mmm, very sweet! I'll take two kilos.

lines.speaker: Endang:
lines.text: Sekalian beli kue buat Dimas, Mbak. Dia suka jajanan pasar.
lines.id: Get some cakes for Dimas while we're here. He loves market snacks.

lines.text: Kue-kue yang warna-warni itu apa namanya, Bu?

lines.text: Yang hijau-hijau itu klepon, isinya gula jawa. Yang berlapis-lapis itu kue lapis.
lines.id: The green ones are klepon, filled with palm sugar. The layered one is kue lapis.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Dari tadi kita bolak-balik, Bu. Kaki saya sudah capek.
lines.id: We've been going back and forth for ages. My feet are killing me.
lines.literal: from earlier we back-and-forth, Mrs. foot my already tired.

lines.speaker: Endang:
lines.text: Ha-ha, itu belum apa-apa. Orang sini ke pasar tiap hari, lho.
lines.id: Ha, that's nothing. People here come to the market every day, you know.

notes: **Pasar Beringharjo** is Yogyakarta's great traditional market, a few minutes' walk from the Kraton. Batik and clothes are near the front; food, fruit and snacks further in; herbs, spices and *jamu* ingredients upstairs. Prices are fair and friendly bargaining is normal, though not for fruit sold by the kilo.

**Pelan-pelan.** Doubling an adjective often turns it into an adverb of manner: *pelan-pelan* (slowly, carefully), *cepat-cepat* (quickly), *baik-baik* (well, properly). *Jangan jauh-jauh* is “don't go too far” — the doubled word softens the order into friendly advice.

**Orangnya banyak banget.** Sarah does not double *orang*, because *banyak* already says there are lots. Indonesian nouns are neutral about number, and doubling is used only when the plurality actually matters. More on this in the second grammar box.

**Monggo** is Javanese for “please, go ahead” and is the market seller's welcome, a bit like “what can I get you?”. She calls Sarah *Mbak* and Bu Endang *Bu*, by age, which is exactly what Sarah should do back.

**Salaknya manis-manis** — “the salak are sweet, every one of them”. A doubled adjective after a plural subject spreads the quality over all the members. *Rumahnya besar-besar* means the houses (in that street) are all big.

**Jajanan pasar** are the traditional snacks sold in markets, mostly made from rice flour, coconut and palm sugar. *Klepon* are green pandan balls that burst with melted *gula jawa* when you bite them — eat them in one go, or wear them.

grammars.title: What doubling does
body: Doubling is not just a plural. Depending on the kind of word, it adds one of five different ideas.

head: Job
Example
English
rows: look around, go out and about, sit around
don't go far at all, it's nothing at all

after: *Jalan-jalan* is the best-known example: not “walk walk” but going out with no particular purpose — to the mall, to the beach, to Malioboro. *Lagi jalan-jalan* is the perfect answer to *Mau ke mana?* when you don't want to explain.
Writing rule: doubled words take a hyphen. 💬 In chat people write *kue2* or *jalan2*, but never in anything formal.

grammars.title: Doubling with a twist
body: Some doubled words change a sound, or add *-an*, and these usually mean “all kinds of” or “back and forth”.

head: Pattern
Example
English
rows: vegetables of all kinds, side dishes
in many layers, of many kinds

after: You cannot make these up yourself; learn them as you meet them. The good news is that there are not very many, and the ones on this page cover most of daily life.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Tugas sekolah Dimas
dialogs.intro: Sunday afternoon. Dimas appears at Sarah's door with a sheet of cardboard, a pair of scissors and a very serious face.

lines.speaker: Dimas:
lines.text: Mbak Sarah, bantuin aku, dong. Aku ada tugas dari Bu Guru.
lines.id: Mbak Sarah, help me, please. I've got homework from my teacher.
lines.literal: Miss Sarah, help-[-in] me, [dong]. I have task from Mrs Teacher.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Tugas apa, Dimas?
lines.id: What homework, Dimas?

lines.speaker: Dimas:
lines.text: Disuruh bikin poster tentang buah-buahan Indonesia. Harus warna-warni.

lines.text: Gampang. Kemarin Mbak beli salak di Beringharjo. Kita gambar salak, ya?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Snake fruit. Kulitnya kayak sisik ular.
lines.id: Snake fruit. Its skin is like snake scales.
lines.literal: snake fruit. skin-its like scale snake.

lines.speaker: Dimas:
lines.text: Hiii! Teman-temanku pasti kaget.

notes: **Bantuin.** The *-in* ending is Jakarta speech (you will study it properly in Unit 19), but children all over Indonesia pick it up from television. Standard is *bantu* or *membantu*: *Tolong bantu saya.* Bu Endang would say *Tolong dibantu, Mbak* — the soft passive request from Unit 6.

**Disuruh bikin poster.** *Disuruh* is “to be told to”, the passive of *menyuruh*; it is how every Indonesian child describes homework. 💬 *Bikin* is the everyday *membuat*, “to make”, and you will hear it far more often than the standard word.

**Kemarin Mbak beli salak.** Talking to a child, Sarah calls herself *Mbak* instead of *aku* or *saya*. Adults do this all the time with children: a mother says *Ibu*, a teacher says *Bu Guru*, an older sister says *Mbak* or *Kakak*. It sounds warm, not odd.

**Motongnya pelan-pelan.** 💬 *Motong* is the spoken *memotong*, the nasal form from Unit 3, and *-nya* turns it into “the cutting”: “do the cutting slowly”. *Jangan sampai* means “make sure you don't”, literally “don't let it get to the point where”.
**Asyik!** — “cool!”, “yay!”. *Hiii!* is the sound of a child who is delighted to be disgusted. *Teman-temanku* is doubled because Dimas means his classmates, a whole set of particular people.

**Eyang** is the Javanese word for grandparent, and Dimas uses it for Bu Endang. In Javanese families you will also hear *Eyang Putri* or *Uti* for grandmother and *Eyang Kakung* or *Akung* for grandfather; elsewhere it is *Nenek* and *Kakek*.

grammars.title: When not to double
body: Most Indonesian nouns are simply not marked for number, and doubling is optional. As soon as another word already shows the number, doubling becomes wrong.
after: So when do you double a noun? When there are many and they are varied or separate, and nothing else in the sentence says so: *Rumah-rumah di sini tua* (the houses round here are old). If in doubt, don't — an undoubled noun is never wrong.

sections.title: Market words that come in pairs

blocks.text: Food in a market is usually talked about in bulk, as categories, and categories love doubling. These are the words on the signs and in the sellers' mouths.

head: Indonesian
English
Examples
rows: gifts brought home from a trip

blocks.text: *Oleh-oleh* is a serious social obligation. Anyone who comes back from a trip is expected to bring something for colleagues and neighbours, and in Yogya that something is almost always a box of *bakpia*.
Some words exist only in doubled form; the single half means nothing, or something else entirely. They are not plurals: *kupu-kupu* is one butterfly or many.

blocks.title: Doubled goodbyes and good wishes
items: *Hati-hati, ya!* — take care (said to anyone leaving, especially on a motorbike)
*Pelan-pelan saja.* — take your time, no rush
*Tidak apa-apa.* 💬 *Nggak apa-apa, gapapa* — it's fine, never mind

Once you've harvested, send her some of the chillies while you're at it!
